summary:
Sections 153 to 155 of the Penal Code criminalise sex between men. Anal intercourse carries up to fourteen years' imprisonment, attempts and assault with intent to commit it up to seven years, and acts of gross indecency between males up to five years. Sex between women is not an offence.

The provisions are not enforced. A 2015 US State Department human rights report recorded no prosecutions under them, and no prosecution of an LGBTQ person under these sections has been reported.

No constitutional or statutory non-discrimination protection covers sexual orientation or gender identity generally. Article 15(3) of the Constitution bars discrimination by reference to race, place of origin, political opinions, colour and creed. The Employment and Industrial Relations Code 2015, Article 107(2)(b), has prohibited employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation since 2015; gender discrimination is prohibited only in employment, and that protection is poorly enforced.

The Marriage Act (Cap 54) does not expressly forbid recognition of marriages between people of the same sex but is written on the assumption that the partners are of the opposite sex; its restrictions address relatives, parties under 16, and bigamy. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no clear route to recognition.

Kiribati has a recognised gender-variant social role, the binabinaaine, also recorded as pinapinaaine in Tuvalu and documented by Besnier (2014). Its presence indicates social space for gender diversity that is distinct from the criminal-law position.
tangentialFactors:
At the 21st session of the Universal Periodic Review, France, Slovenia and Chile urged Kiribati to decriminalise homosexuality. The Kiribati delegation did not respond to those recommendations but said it was considering Uruguay's advice to adopt legislation prohibiting discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual identity and sexual orientation.

In November 2016 Kiribati voted at the UN General Assembly to retain the Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; the amendment to defund the mandate failed 84 to 77. Kiribati and Sri Lanka were the only states criminalising homosexuality to vote that way.
localsOnly:
Employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation has been prohibited since 2015 under Article 107(2)(b) of the Employment and Industrial Relations Code 2015. Gender discrimination is prohibited only in employment, and enforcement of that provision is poor.

The Marriage Act (Cap 54) governs marriage recognition locally. It does not expressly bar recognition of same-sex marriages, but its terms assume the parties are of the opposite sex.
outOfScopeNotes:
Reporting on societal treatment is inconsistent. The 2015 US State Department report recorded no reported societal discrimination or violence against LGBTQ people; other material states that lesbians may face violence and discrimination. Neither account is quantified, and no trans-specific violence data for Kiribati was identified.

No sourced information was identified on document and gender-marker rules for trans travellers, on entry or visa screening, on bathroom or facilities access, or on access to transition-related care.
